reading.rtitle: The Night the Lights Went Out
paras: The play started at eight, and five minutes later the room was doing exactly what a theater room does. Two hundred people were sitting still. An actor was walking towards the front of the stage. Somewhere in the third row a phone was ringing, and its owner was looking for it in a bag and pretending it belonged to somebody else.

At quarter past eight the lights went out. Not only the stage lights -- all of them, including the small green ones above the doors. For about four seconds nobody moved, because nobody realized what was happening. Then a woman in the second row laughed, and suddenly everybody was talking at once.

The actor did not leave. He was standing in the same place when the emergency lights came on, and he simply carried on from the line he had reached a moment before. Somebody found a flashlight and held it on him from the side. He performed the next twenty minutes with one light and no microphone, and afterwards he said it was the best audience of his life, because for once nobody was looking at a phone.

The lights came back at twenty to nine. The play finished forty minutes late, and nobody left early. While everybody was waiting for the bus outside, four people who did not know each other were still arguing about whether the dark part had been better.
reading.source: A night at the theater, written for this lesson.

choices: To explain what to do when the electricity stops in a public place.
To tell one night as a story: what was already going on, and the thing that walked in and stopped it.
To review a play and say whether it is worth seeing.

items.situation: Describe the room before the lights went out. Two things at the same time.
tips: Two hundred people were sitting still and an actor was walking towards the stage.
Background needs was or were plus the -ing form. Never leave was out.

items.situation: Now say the thing that broke it, in the past simple.
tips: At quarter past eight the lights went out.
The event that interrupts is never in the -ing form.

items.situation: Put both halves in one sentence, using when.
tips: He was standing in the same place when the emergency lights came on.
Background first with was or were, then when plus past simple.

items.situation: Say two long things happening at the same time, using while.
tips: While everybody was waiting for the bus, four people were arguing about the play.
While goes with the long one. Both halves take was or were.

items.situation: Ask me what I was doing, and then answer your own question.
tips: What were you doing when it happened? I was watching something on my phone.
Question order: were plus you plus the -ing form.

items.situation: Tell me about a night that did not go as planned, in three sentences.
tips: I was waiting for a friend at the restaurant when she called and cancelled.
One sentence of background, one of what happened, one of what you did next.

listenings.text: Everybody in my family remembers where they were, and none of us remembers the same thing. My mother says she was cooking. My brother says she was on the phone and the pan was burning. I was nine. I was lying on the floor doing homework I was not really doing, and the television was on with the sound down. Then the phone rang and my mother went very quiet, and my brother and I looked at each other, because children always know before anybody tells them. What I remember is not the news itself. I remember that the fan was turning, that somebody outside was cutting the grass, and that my pencil rolled under the sofa and I never got it back. Thirty years later I could draw that room for you. I could not tell you a single word anybody said.

There is a good reason why you remember the background of a bad moment better than the moment itself. While something ordinary is going on, your brain is barely writing anything down. It is running on the idea that today is the same as yesterday, so there is nothing to save. Then something breaks the pattern, and for about ninety seconds it writes down everything, including the parts that do not matter at all. The smell. The shoes. What was playing. So the fan, the grass outside, the pencil under the sofa are not sentimental details. They are the last frame of the ordinary, kept because it was still on the desk when the alarm went off. It is also why people say the strangest sentence in the language. I remember exactly what I was doing. Not what happened. What they were doing.
